extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in journalism, media ethics, and AI in news
extracted.subtask_short: reporting on AI use in journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards implied by a news story about media organizations using AI to create content — focused on how newsrooms should disclose, attribute, verify, and supervise AI-assisted or AI-generated journalism. Useful for editors, publishers, and readers evaluating newsroom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about use of AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Media companies should be explicit about the role of technology in creating articles rather than hiding it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page quotations: 'the mistake is in trying to hide it, and in doing it poorly.' Examples of good practice: Buzzfeed attributing a travel article to 'Emma Heegar and Buzzy the Robot' and AP placing a note at the end of stories explaining technology's role. CNET later made clear when AI was being used after the experiment was discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness / avoid deception
rubrics_metrics.description: If you claim to be in the 'truth-telling business,' newsrooms should not tell lies or keep secrets about content production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quote: 'If you want to be in the truth-telling business, which journalists claim they do, you shouldn't tell lies.' Hiding AI use is characterized as a form of lying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish computer-written stories under fake people/bylines
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should not publish computer-written stories attributed to fictitious authors or personas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sports Illustrated Union demand: 'including not publishing computer-written stories by fake people.' The Futurism investigation found author portraits that were AI-generated and bylines for authors that could not be identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and accurate author attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Bylines should accurately reflect who wrote the story (human author, staff, contractor, or AI-assisted), and the attribution should be discoverable by readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gannett labeled AI pieces 'LedeAI'; Buzzfeed used dual human-and-AI attribution. CNET initially attributed to 'CNET Money Staff' with limited disclosure; later clarified. Avoid using opaque pen names or misleading attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose technology involvement in individual stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an explicit disclosure in the story (for example, a note at the end) that explains technology's role and the data or vendors used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AP example: 'The Associated Press created this story using technology provided by Data Skrive and data from Sportradar.' Such notes make AI involvement explicit and transparent to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and quality control for AI-generated or AI-assisted content
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure rigorous fact-checking and human oversight, because machine-generated articles have produced errors requiring corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Gannett pausing experiments after errors; CNET reported corrections for several machine-generated stories. Human editors should verify output and correct mistakes before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting and oversight of third-party content providers
rubrics_metrics.description: When outsourcing content production to third-party companies, publishers must verify claims that content was written and edited by humans and maintain editorial control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sports Illustrated said AdVon Commerce assured them writers were human; Futurism's report contradicted that. Publishers should not blindly trust vendor assurances and should audit vendor practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt remediation and transparency after problems are discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: If AI misuse or misattribution is discovered, remove or correct the content, end problematic partnerships if necessary, and conduct internal investigations while informing readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sports Illustrated removed the content and ended the partnership while investigating. CNET publicly acknowledged the experiment and its corrections after discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to basic journalistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should commit to and adhere to established journalistic standards (accuracy, transparency, accountability) even when using new technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union call: 'We demand the company commit to adhering to basic journalistic standards,' applying these principles to AI-era practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify provenance of author photos and profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm that author portraits and profile content are authentic and not AI-generated or taken from third-party AI-portrait services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Futurism found a pictured author on a website that sells AI-generated portraits; publishers should verify images used for author profiles to avoid fake personas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be upfront with readers about experiments using AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss with readers when experiments with AI are being run, what their purpose is, and how they affect content production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gannett and CNET only discussed experiments after discovery; the article argues some unpleasant publicity could have been avoided if newsrooms had been explicit about technology's role from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate AI-native content from AI-enhanced human work
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly label whether a piece is 'AI-native' (content that could not be produced without AI) or 'enhanced by AI but created by humans.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buzzfeed's statement: 'We'll be developing content that is AI-native ... and things that are enhanced by AI but created by humans.' Publishers should communicate the nature of AI's creative role to readers.
